passage: The last bus to the hostel left in twenty minutes, and Zeenat still hadn't decided. Dilnaz stood at the stop with her arms crossed, rain dripping from her umbrella. "Either you tell your parents you're skipping the cousin's engagement to come to my recital, or I stop talking to you. I mean it." Zeenat felt her stomach drop. The recital mattered to her too, but so did her aunt's house, full of people she loved. "Is this really an either-or?" she asked. "I could come to the second show." Dilnaz looked away. "No. This one." The bus lights swung round the corner, and Zeenat realised she didn't know whether Dilnaz was saying something that hurt, or something she'd take back in the morning.

qa.q: How long until the last bus to the hostel left?
qa.a: The last bus left in twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling as she listened to the ultimatum, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt pressured and unsure, shown by her stomach dropping and her question about whether it was really either-or.

qa.q: What could Zeenat do next before agreeing to anything?
qa.a: She could tell Dilnaz she cares about both events, ask why this show matters so much, and talk again once they are calm and not rushing for a bus.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz see her own ultimatum?
qa.a: Dilnaz may be scared of being left out and this recital may feel like a real need, though it may also be pressure, and only more talk will show which.

grounding: Zeenat faces an ultimatum whose meaning is unclear: a boundary or pressure.

passage: Rajni's brother Vishal had said it at dinner three times that week: "Give up the Pune job offer or don't expect me at your wedding." Rajni carried her plate to the sink, pretending she hadn't heard. In her room she opened the offer letter again. Vishal wasn't shouting, and he wasn't a cruel person. He had raised her after their parents' passing. But every time she talked about the city, he changed the subject or said what she owed the family. She wrote two lists, one headed "What he fears" and one headed "What I want". Then she called her aunt and asked if she could talk. Rajni didn't want to lose her brother, and she didn't want her choice decided by a threat either.

qa.q: How many times had Vishal said it at dinner that week?
qa.a: He had said it three times that week.

qa.q: What is Rajni feeling as she writes her two lists, and what else might be behind Vishal's words?
qa.a: Rajni feels torn, wanting to keep her brother but not to be controlled, while Vishal may truly be afraid of losing her rather than trying to punish her.

qa.q: What did Rajni do that helped?
qa.a: She separated his fears from her wishes on paper and reached out to her aunt for support instead of deciding alone.

qa.q: How might Vishal see the ultimatum?
qa.a: He may see it as a way to keep the family close after their loss, without realising it makes Rajni feel her choices are not respected.

grounding: Rajni faces a 'do this or else' demand that could be either fear or control and seeks support.

passage:
"Delete Karan and Vikram from your phone," Siddharth said. "Or I'm done."
Shalini stared at him. "They're my lab partners."
"You're always laughing at their messages. If you loved me, you'd delete them."
"I do love you. And I'm not deleting my lab partners."
"Then choose."
"Sid, last month you said you'd leave if I went to my cousin's wedding without you. Now this."
"Because I care."
"Caring doesn't sound like 'choose or I leave' every few weeks."
He grabbed his jacket. "Fine. Call me when you've decided."
Shalini sat very still after he left, her hands shaking. Then she called her sister.
"Didi? Can you come over? I think something's not right."
"I'm coming now," Didi said. "Don't answer him till I'm there. We'll talk it through together."

qa.q: Who did Siddharth want Shalini to delete from her phone?
qa.a: Karan and Vikram.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling after Siddharth left?
qa.a: She was shaken and scared, her hands shaking, and unsure what was happening, which is why she called her sister.

qa.q: Why was calling her sister a wise step?
qa.a: The ultimatums were repeated and controlling, not a fair boundary, so getting support from a trusted person helped Shalini think clearly and stay safe.

qa.q: How did Didi respond when Shalini called?
qa.a: She came straight away, told Shalini not to answer him until she arrived, and offered to talk it through together.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising repeated ultimatums from a partner as pressure and control, and seeking support.

passage: The ultimatum I think about most came from my friend Irawati in our second year. I'm Rajni, and back then I was lying a lot. Small things: that I'd return her notes, that I'd be at her play, that I'd pay back the auto fare. One evening she sat me down. "Rajni, I love you. But if you lie to me one more time, I'm stepping back from this friendship." I was furious. I told her she was being dramatic, controlling. I cried to my roommate that night. But my roommate asked, "Is she telling you what to do, or telling you what she'll do?" That stopped me. Irawati wasn't ordering me around. She was saying what she needed to stay. I could choose. I chose to stop lying, clumsily at first. We're still friends. I've learned that some ultimatums are just someone's honest limit.

qa.q: What did Irawati say she would do if Rajni lied again?
qa.a: She would step back from the friendship.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel when Irawati gave the ultimatum?
qa.a: Rajni felt furious and hurt at first, calling Irawati dramatic and controlling, and cried to the roommate that night.

qa.q: What question helped Rajni see the ultimatum differently?
qa.a: The roommate's question: is she telling you what to do, or what she'll do? It showed Irawati was stating a boundary, leaving Rajni free to choose.

qa.q: How did Irawati likely see her own ultimatum?
qa.a: As an honest limit about what she needed to stay in the friendship after repeated lies, not as control.

grounding: Shows that some ultimatums state a real boundary and respect the other's choice, unlike pressure or control.

passage:
Counsellor's note, college wellbeing centre, Monday.
Anjali, a final-year student, came in today, very tense. Her father has told her that if she does not agree to marry a man the family has chosen by Diwali, she should "never come home again". Her mother has stopped speaking to her. She said, "Maybe he's just upset. Maybe it's normal." I asked whether she feels she has a real choice. She said no, and that she is afraid to go home for the holidays. We talked about the difference between a parent stating a limit and pressure that removes her choice and makes her afraid. I explained that she does not have to decide anything today. With her permission, I contacted the college's women's cell and a legal aid counsellor, and gave her the helpline number. She will stay in the hostel over the holiday. I will see her on Wednesday.
— Rekha

qa.q: When does Anjali's father want her to agree by?
qa.a: By Diwali.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling during the session?
qa.a: She was tense and afraid to go home, and unsure whether her father's pressure was normal.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor take that were wise?
qa.a: She explained Anjali didn't have to decide today, connected her with the women's cell and legal aid with her permission, gave the helpline and arranged for her to stay in the hostel.

qa.q: How does Rekha see the father's ultimatum?
qa.a: Rekha sees it as pressure that removes Anjali's choice and makes her afraid, not simply a parent stating a limit.

grounding: Shows a young adult facing a family ultimatum that is coercion, and a counsellor helping her find support where fear is present.

passage:
Wednesday, 11 p.m.
Two ultimatums in one day. Writing them down so I can think.
Morning: Mohan, my flatmate, said, "If you smoke on the balcony again, I'll have to move out. The smoke gets into my room and I can't breathe properly." Annoying, but fair. It's about his health, and he's leaving me a clear choice. I'll stop.
Evening: Bhavna, on the phone, said, "Stop talking to Anjum or we're done. And I want to see your chats." When I asked why, she said I obviously didn't love her enough. It's the third time this month she's said "do this or I leave", and each time the list gets longer. I noticed my hands were cold, and I felt scared to text Anjum back.
That's the difference, I think. Mohan's is a boundary about his own room. Bhavna's is about controlling who I talk to. I called Didi at ten. She listened, and said I can stay at hers this weekend while I work it out.
Vikas

qa.q: Why did Mohan give his ultimatum?
qa.a: The smoke gets into his room and he can't breathe properly.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel after Bhavna's call?
qa.a: Vikas felt scared and uneasy, with cold hands and fear of texting Anjum back, sensing control rather than a fair request.

qa.q: What did Vikas do after noticing the difference?
qa.a: Wrote both ultimatums down to think clearly and called Didi the same night, who offered a place to stay that weekend.

qa.q: How does Mohan's ultimatum look from Mohan's side?
qa.a: As a necessary boundary to protect his health in his own room, leaving Vikas a fair choice.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult telling apart an ultimatum that states a real boundary from one that pressures and controls, and seeking support when fear appears.
